fields.Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "Two Nativity Stories That Refuse to Fit Together", "body": "John McHugh traces his research back to seventh grade, when a nun named Sister Regina had him read the birth stories in Matthew and Luke one after the other. Matthew has astrologers, a moving star, treasures and a house. Luke has a census, a caravanserai, swaddling clothes, a manger, shepherds and a heavenly army. Neither mentions the other. Leaning on Raymond E. Brown and William F. Albright, McHugh argues the two accounts are irreconcilable, were appended last to both gospels around the mid 80s AD, and rest on no corroborating eyewitness at all."}, {"title": "Why Nobody Else Wrote Down the Christmas Star", "body": "Chance Garton and McHugh pick apart the star's behavior. Babylonian astrologers see it in the east, travel roughly 900 miles to Jerusalem over about three months, consult Herod, then watch the star hang a left, move six miles to Bethlehem and park over one house like a drone with a spotlight. They argue that in an era when calendars were kept by court astronomers using ephemerides, such an object could not have been missed. Yet no Canaanite, Greek or Roman source records it. McHugh also notes Matthew skips his usual fulfillment formula here, which he uses when he means business."}, {"title": "Lamashi and the Art of Reading the Sky", "body": "The heart of the episode is Lamashi, or constellation writing, paired with the Greek idea of catasterism, the belief that pictures in the stars proved events had truly happened on earth. Babylonian scholars called the sky heavenly writing and treated themselves as its readers. Because cuneiform carries roughly 600 signs, each with layers of Sumerian logograms and homophones, a single sign like mul could mean star, writing, arrow, god, field or feeling elated. Quoting A. R. George and Scott Noegel, McHugh explains that finding a pun in a divine name counted as revelation, not comedy."}, {"title": "Regulus, the Manger and the Pregnant Virgin", "body": "McHugh places the whole nativity in one patch of sky spanning Virgo, Leo and Cancer. Babylonian tablets call Regulus Sharu, a word that reads as both king and infant, which is why the Latin name means little king. Virgo's original title Absin means furrow, but alternate readings give virgin and, he suggests, bitter sea, the same Mar Yam behind Miriam or Mary. The western stars of Virgo carry Eru, to be pregnant. M44 in Cancer is Praesepe, the manger. Pregnant virgin, infant king and feeding trough sit together, and McHugh says Matthew and Luke read that tableau as history."}, {"title": "Wordplay Behind Every Detail of the Story", "body": "McHugh walks through the puns line by line. Leo's title labu also means to wrap up, and Regulus can be read shar, a fine regal cloth, giving she wrapped him in cloth. Bootes as Uthul yields shepherd, its northwestern stars yield flock, Orion gives shepherd and angel of the Lord, and Libra's Sumerian spelling yields army of heaven. Spica's wheat produces frankincense, Absin's bitter produces myrrh, and Regulus produces house, gold and treasures. Chance Garton links the same tableau to Adonis, born of a mother turned into a myrrh tree, and to Dionysus, Manu and Bacchus."}]
fields.Intro Paragraph 1: Archeo-Astronomer & linguistic code-breaker John McHugh returns to InnerVerse for our yearly Christmas special! Tune in to learn about the Celestial Code of Scripture that underlies all miracle stories of religion and mythology, and how the miraculous "Star of Bethlehem" of Jesus' nativity in the book of Matthew may be the Royal Star Regulus, in the Leo Constellation. Wordplay within sacred writings reveals the "secrets of the gods," and with the information in this episode, you'll be privy to the archaic astral cipher, to better understand the basis for divine revelation.
